summary: Analysis of 2026 campaign finance. Republican party committees and Super PACs held far more cash (about $1 billion versus $514 million), but Democratic candidates raised much more in individual contributions, the only finance data FLIPR uses. Because Super PACs pay more per ad, Democrats' candidate dollars go further. The piece restates how FLIPR treats individual contributions as grassroots support with in-state weighting, and how late entrants are handled, including Troy Jackson being credited with half of Graham Platner's fundraising. Silver Bulletin's view is that money is overrated in high-profile races.

findings.statement: Individual contributions to candidates are the only campaign-finance data in FLIPR's fancy fundamentals. They are treated as a measure of grassroots support, so contributions from the candidate's own state or district get more weight; party committee, PAC and Super PAC money and ad reservations are not used.
findings.evidence_quote: Democrats also have an advantage when it comes to individual contributions, which is the only campaign finance data that feeds into FLIPR’s “fancy fundamentals” estimates.

findings.statement: FLIPR gives late-entrant candidates 'amnesty' on fundraising: Troy Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner in Maine and had not yet filed a report, gets credit for half of what Platner raised.
findings.evidence_quote: The model gives him amnesty as a late entrant, so he gets credit for half of what Graham Platner raised.

findings.statement: In-state shares of itemized individual contributions to 2026 Senate candidates were similar by party: 36 percent for Democrats and 38 percent for Republicans.
findings.evidence_quote: 36 percent of itemized individual contributions to Democratic Senate candidates are in-state, compared to 38 percent for Republicans.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin's view is that money is closer to overrated than underrated, at least in high-profile campaigns like Senate and presidential races, where earned media matters more than paid media and diminishing returns set in on saturated airwaves.
findings.evidence_quote: Our view at Silver Bulletin is that money is closer to overrated than underrated

findings.statement: Super PACs often pay several times what campaigns do for comparable broadcast TV ads, so ad spending does not equal ad impressions and party or PAC cash is less efficient than candidate dollars.
findings.evidence_quote: Super PACs often pay several times what campaigns do for comparable broadcast TV ads.

findings.statement: 2026 individual-contribution gaps cited as drivers of FLIPR fancy fundamentals: Talarico $66M vs Paxton $9M in Texas; Brown $25M ahead of Husted in Ohio; Peltola $12M ahead of Sullivan in Alaska; El-Sayed $7M ahead of Rogers in Michigan. Totals: Democratic House nominees $648M vs Republicans $437M; Democratic Senate nominees $329M vs $133M.

political_insights.insight: In 2026 Republicans dominated party and Super PAC cash (MAGA Inc. alone $416M) while Democrats dominated candidate fundraising via grassroots platforms like ActBlue; the DNC itself was weak with $18M debt.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Party-committee finances are a poor proxy for candidate strength.

political_insights.insight: Democratic challengers in competitive House districts outraised GOP incumbents, consistent with an enthusiasm advantage.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Challenger fundraising relative to incumbents signals wave conditions.

references.description: Cook Political Report Q2 2026 fundraising analysis

open_questions: How in-state contributions are weighted relative to total in the fundraising variable (5x per methodology).
